questions.q: In this case study, why is the executive statement "the system cannot be the reason an angry customer waits longer during our worst week" not yet a usable NFR?
options: Because executives are never a valid source for NFRs
Because it is vague and unconditional, exactly like the kind of input Lesson 8 describes needing to be translated into a specific metric, target, and condition before it's testable
Because this statement is actually a functional requirement, not an NFR
Because it only applies to the compliance NFR category
questions.explain: Like 'it needs to be fast' or 'it can't go down,' this statement names an outcome without a specific metric, numeric target, or load condition attached — exactly the elicitation starting point Lesson 8 says needs translating into something testable.

questions.q: Why are performance, scalability, and reliability identified as the dominant NFR categories for this specific retailer, while compliance is comparatively light?
options: Because compliance NFRs never apply to Service Cloud implementations
Because security is irrelevant to any Service Cloud implementation
Because performance always outranks every other NFR category in every scenario

Because this scenario has no regulated data category driving it, while the business's real risk is volume-driven: spike performance, transaction-volume scalability, and integration reliability during exactly those spikes
questions.explain: Not every org needs the same NFR emphasis — this case study's finding is that this specific business's risk profile is dominated by volume-driven pressures (performance, scalability, reliability) rather than a regulated-data compliance driver, which would weigh differently for a different kind of organization.

questions.q: Why was case-assignment scoring moved to an asynchronous path in this case study's design decision?
options: Because routing-rule evaluation and skill matching running inline on every case insert threatens the synchronous save's performance target specifically as volume climbs during a spike, so moving it async keeps the save fast
Because asynchronous Apex is always required by Salesforce for any Service Cloud implementation
Because the e-commerce integration requires all Apex to run asynchronously
Because asynchronous Apex eliminates the need for idempotent design
questions.explain: Following Lesson 9's trace pattern, the performance/scalability pressure during a spike implies that meaningful synchronous work on case insert is a risk — moving assignment scoring async keeps the user-facing save transaction fast even at high volume.

questions.q: Why does the e-commerce integration's Apex endpoint need to upsert against an external reference ID rather than always insert a new case?
options: Because upsert is required by Salesforce governor limits for all integrations
Because insert operations are disabled during a product recall

Because the integration is most likely to retry exactly during the chaotic recall week, and a blind insert on a retried request would create a duplicate case for the same customer complaint — an idempotency requirement from Lesson 5
Because external reference IDs are mandatory fields on the standard Case object
questions.explain: This reliability requirement follows directly from Lesson 5's idempotency principle — a retried request during the exact period of highest integration stress must not create a duplicate case, which is exactly what upserting against an external reference ID prevents.

questions.q: What trade-off does Lesson 11's conflict lens identify in this case study's asynchronous-assignment decision?
options: That asynchronous assignment is strictly better in every respect, with no trade-off at all

That moving assignment fully asynchronous slightly delays the moment an agent is actually notified, trading a small amount of per-case latency for overall system stability during the spike — a trade-off that should be named explicitly and signed off, not left implicit
That asynchronous assignment violates the compliance NFR for this organization
That asynchronous assignment is only possible in a Full sandbox, not in production
questions.explain: Even a design decision that solves the dominant risk (stability under spike load) introduces a smaller, real trade-off (slightly delayed agent notification) — exactly the kind of conflict Lesson 11 says should be named and explicitly approved rather than left as an unstated side effect.
